In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the performance of estimators for treatment effects and program evaluation depends on the design of the evaluation study, i.e. sample size, effect heterogeneity and the selection into treatment, and the choice of the estimator, i.e. whether the estimator is parametric, semparametric, or nonparametric.
no single estimator outperforms the others across all designs considered.
the performance of a treatment estimator depends strongly on the specific data-generating mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best performing estimator in terms of RMSE is a doubly robust estimator based on a nonparametric propensity score and a linear model for the outcome.
, for our designs and estimators considered, there is no clear winner in terms of average RMSE.
nonparametric propensity score methods are a good choice for estimating average treatment effects in small samples, while parametric propensity score methods perform better in large samples.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single best estimator for treatment effects.
nonparametric estimator choice is crucial in practice, as there is considerable variability in performance across estimators, which is driven by the simulation design considered.
